introduction.p: In , a single bound independent of x controlled a whole interval. The M-test extends that idea from power series to arbitrary series of functions. This optional section uses the Cauchy criterion from .

subsection.title: A numerical majorant controls a function series
subsection.p: For functions f_n:D\to\mathbb R, the series \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x) converges uniformly to F on D when its partial sums S_N(x) satisfy: for every \varepsilon>0, there is one N_0 such that |F(x)-S_N(x)|<\varepsilon for all N\ge N_0 and every x\in D.

statement.p: Suppose |f_n(x)|\le M_n for every x\in D, where M_n\ge0 and \sum M_n converges. Then \sum f_n(x) converges absolutely at every point and uniformly on D. Its remainder satisfies

The Cauchy criterion makes the right side arbitrarily small for sufficiently large p, independently of q and x. Letting q\to\infty yields the remainder bound. The tails of the convergent majorant series tend to zero, so this same bound proves uniform convergence.

subsection.p: If each f_n is continuous, the uniform-limit theorem makes F continuous. On a finite closed interval, the integration theorem in then gives \int_a^b F=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\int_a^b f_n. To differentiate term by term, one needs additional control of the derivative series; the M-test for the original terms alone is insufficient.

subsection.title: Examples, error bounds, and limitations

example.title: A uniformly convergent trigonometric series
example.p: For every real x, |\sin(nx)/n^2|\le1/n^2. Since \sum1/n^2 converges, the function

is continuous, and the integral-test tail bound gives |F(x)-S_N(x)|\le1/N for every real x. On any [0,b], term-by-term integration is valid and yields \int_0^bF(x)\,dx=\sum_{n=1}^\infty(1-\cos(nb))/n^3. This conclusion uses no Fourier-series theorem.

example.title: The power-series safety margin revisited
example.p: If \sum c_n(x-a)^n has radius R>0, fix 0<r<R. On |x-a|\le r, take M_n=|c_n|r^n. This numerical series converges because r lies inside the radius. The M-test proves uniform convergence on that smaller interval. An endpoint at distance R requires its own analysis.

warning.title: Uniform convergence does not control every operation
warning.p: The series \sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(n^2x)/n^2 passes the M-test on \mathbb R. But its formally differentiated series is \sum\cos(n^2x), which diverges at x=0 because its terms equal 1. The original M-test does not justify that differentiation.

subsection.p: The M-test is sufficient, not necessary. A function series with constant terms f_n(x)=(-1)^{n-1}/n converges uniformly on any set, because the alternating-series remainder is at most 1/(N+1) independently of x. But any nonnegative majorant M_n must be at least 1/n, so no convergent majorant exists.

statement.p: Prove uniform convergence of \sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n/n^2 on [-1,1] and give a remainder bound. Then show that \sum_{n=0}^\infty(1-x)x^n converges pointwise on [0,1] but not uniformly.

hint.p: Use M_n=1/n^2 and remainder at most 1/N. The second sum equals 1 for x<1 and 0 at x=1. Its continuous partial sums cannot converge uniformly to this discontinuous limit; alternatively, their error for x<1 is x^{N+1}, whose supremum is 1.
